title: Base rates
objectives: See how a rare condition makes most positive tests false
Compute $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$ from a base rate and two test rates
Explain why the same test means different things in different groups

screens.prose: A condition affects 1 in 100 people. A test spots 90% of cases, and wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. Your test comes back positive.
screens.question: Roughly how likely is it that you have the condition?

options.why: You read the test's hit rate as your chance. That turns the condition around.
You split the difference between the test and the base rate. Compare the two paths that end in a positive.
That is the chance before the test. A positive result should raise it.

hints.text: Which two paths end in a positive test?
Compare these two paths. Which is bigger?
Condition and positive: $0.01 \times 0.9 = 0.009$. Healthy and positive: $0.99 \times 0.05 = 0.0495$.

feedback.correct: Most positives come from healthy people.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two paths that end in a positive.

explain.text: Condition and positive is $0.01 \times 0.9 = 0.009$. Healthy and positive is $0.99 \times 0.05 = 0.0495$, over five times bigger. So only about 15% of positives have the condition.

screens.prose: Keep the same test and change how common the condition is. The left bar is the chance before the test; the right bar is the chance after a positive.

state.caption: Base rate 1%: after a positive, the chance is 0.15

derive.caption: Base rate {{round(base*100)}}%: after a positive, the chance is {{fixed(0.9*base/(0.9*base + 0.05*(1 - base)), 2)}}

screens.question: Slide the base rate up. Where does a positive first make the condition more likely than not?

options.why: At 1% the right bar is only about 0.15. Slide further.
At 30% the right bar is already near 0.89. It crossed 0.5 much earlier.
At 50% the right bar is about 0.95. Slide back down to find where it crosses 0.5.

hints.text: Watch the right bar as you slide. When does it pass 0.5?
Try 5% and then 6%.
At 5% the right bar reads 0.49. At 6% it reads 0.53.

feedback.correct: The right bar crosses 0.5 between 5% and 6%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide slowly and read the right bar.

explain.text: The right bar climbs fast at first: 0.15 at 1%, about 0.5 by 5%, 0.89 at 30%. The test never changed. Only how common the condition is changed.

screens.prose: How common the condition is before any test, 1% here, is called the **base rate**. Back to a base rate of 1%.
screens.question: What is $P(+)$, the chance a random person tests positive? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Two paths end in a positive test.
Multiply along each path, then add.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply along each path that ends in a positive, then add.

byKey.ill-only: You counted only people with the condition. Healthy people test positive too.
byKey.unweighted: You added 5% without weighting it by the 99% who are healthy: use $0.99 \times 0.05$.
byKey.rates: You added the two rates. Each needs weighting by how many people it applies to.

explain.text: Two paths end in a positive: $0.009 + 0.0495 = 0.0585$. Almost 6 people in 100 test positive, but only 1 in 100 has the condition.

screens.prose: Same tree, base rate 1%. Now put the number on the hook's question.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of the condition given a positive

hints.text: Which path do you want, and which paths make the condition?
Put this path over both positive paths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the condition-and-positive path by all positive paths.

byKey.inverse: That is the test's hit rate, $P(+ \mid \text{condition})$. You want the condition given a positive.
byKey.joint: That is condition and positive together. Divide by $P(+) = 0.0585$.
byKey.base: That is the base rate. The positive should raise it.

explain.text: $0.009 / 0.0585 = \tfrac{2}{13} \approx 0.154$. The positive raised the chance fifteenfold, from 0.01. It is still far from 0.9.

screens.prose: Same tree. A positive result is false when the person is healthy.
screens.question: What share of all positive results are false? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Share of positives that are false

hints.text: False positives come from one path. Which?
This path holds the false positives.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the healthy-and-positive path over all positive paths.

byKey.fp-rate: That is the false-positive rate among healthy people. The question asks about positives.
byKey.true-share: That is the share of positives that are true. Take the other path.
byKey.joint: That is healthy and positive among everyone. Divide by all positives, 0.0585.

explain.text: $0.0495 / 0.0585 \approx 0.85$. When a condition is rare, most positive tests are false. The healthy crowd is so large that 5% of it outnumbers the true cases.

screens.prose: Same test, a different group: here half the people tested have the condition.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$ now? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of the condition given a positive

hints.text: Work out the two positive paths again with 0.5 at the start.
These two paths end in a positive.
$0.5 \times 0.9 = 0.45$ and $0.5 \times 0.05 = 0.025$. Divide 0.45 by their sum.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recompute both positive paths with a base rate of 0.5.

byKey.hit: That is the hit rate alone. The healthy path still adds false positives.
byKey.base: That is the chance before the test. A positive moves it.

explain.text: With a 50% base rate the 0.5 cancels top and bottom: $\dfrac{0.9}{0.9 + 0.05} = \tfrac{18}{19}$. Only the test's two rates are left. This is the edge case where the base rate drops out.

screens.prose: Two clinics use the same test. Clinic A screens everyone: base rate 1%. Clinic B tests only people with symptoms: base rate 30%.

state.caption: The base rate is 1% at clinic A and 30% at clinic B

screens.question: A patient at each clinic tests positive. Whose positive is more likely to be right?

options.text: Equally likely: it is the same test
options.why: You judged the result by the test alone. The base rate differs, and it moves the answer.
Clinic A tests mostly healthy people, so most of its positives are false.

hints.text: Does the base rate appear in the calculation?
The first branch is where the two clinics differ.

feedback.correct: Clinic B tests people far more likely to be ill, so its positives are mostly true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$ at each clinic.

byKey.same: You ignored the base rate: the same test, so the same answer. But clinic A's positives are 85% false and clinic B's only 11%.

explain.text: Clinic A: $0.009 / 0.0585 \approx 0.15$. Clinic B: $0.27 / 0.305 \approx 0.89$. A test result means nothing without the base rate of the people tested.

screens.prose: Every time you weighed the same two paths. With base rate $b$, hit rate $h$ and false-positive rate $f$: $$P(\text{condition} \mid +) = \frac{h\,b}{h\,b + f\,(1 - b)}$$
screens.question: With $b = 0.01$, $h = 0.9$ and $f = 0.05$, which term on the bottom is bigger?

options.why: $0.009$ is smaller than $0.0495$. The healthy group is 99 times larger, which outweighs the low rate.
One is more than five times the other: $0.0495$ against $0.009$.

hints.text: Work out each term.

feedback.correct: When $b$ is small, the false positives swamp the true ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both terms with these numbers.

explain.text: $f\,(1 - b) = 0.0495$ beats $h\,b = 0.009$. A small rate applied to a huge group beats a big rate applied to a tiny group. That is why rare conditions make most positives false.

screens.prose: A bank's fraud model flags 95% of fraudulent payments and 1% of genuine ones. Only 0.2% of payments are fraud. A payment is flagged.
screens.question: What is the chance the flagged payment is fraud? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance a flagged payment is fraud

hints.text: Which two paths end in a flag?
Both of these paths end in a flag.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the fraud-and-flagged path over both flagged paths.

byKey.inverse: That is the share of fraud the model catches. You want the share of flags that are fraud.
byKey.joint: That is fraud and flagged together. Divide by every flag, 0.01188.
byKey.spec: That is the share of genuine payments the model passes. It is not about flagged payments.

explain.text: Fraud and flagged is 0.0019; genuine and flagged is 0.00998. So only about 16% of flags are fraud. With a 0.2% base rate, even a 1% false-alarm rate buries the real cases.

screens.prose: A quant tests many candidate strategies. About 5% have a real edge; the rest are noise. A backtest passes 90% of real strategies and, by luck, 10% of noise. One strategy passes.
screens.question: What is the chance it has a real edge? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of a real edge given a pass

hints.text: Which two paths end in a pass?
Both of these paths end in a pass.
$0.05 \times 0.9 = 0.045$ and $0.95 \times 0.1 = 0.095$. Divide 0.045 by their sum.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the real-and-passes path over both paths that pass.

byKey.inverse: That is the chance a real strategy passes. You want the chance a passing strategy is real.
byKey.joint: That is real and passing together. Divide by every pass, 0.14.
byKey.base: That is the share of real strategies before the backtest. A pass should raise it.
byKey.luck: That is the chance noise passes. It belongs in the bottom of the fraction.

explain.text: Real and passing is 0.045; noise and passing is 0.095. So a pass leaves about a one-in-three chance of a real edge. When most candidates are noise, most backtest winners are noise too.

ideas: The base rate is how common something is before the evidence. It belongs in every calculation.
When the condition is rare, false positives from the large healthy group outnumber true positives.
With a 50% base rate, the base rate cancels and only the test's two rates matter.

formula.name: Posterior from a base rate
formula.note: $b$ is the base rate, $h$ the hit rate, $f$ the false-positive rate.

summary.trap: Judging a positive by the test alone ignores the base rate. The same test means about 0.15 in one clinic and 0.89 in another.

quiz.prose: Only 5% of chart setups lead to a real breakout. A pattern appears before 60% of real breakouts and before 10% of setups that fail.
quiz.question: The pattern appears. What is the chance of a real breakout? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of a breakout given the pattern

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the two paths that end with the pattern.

byKey.inverse: That is the chance of the pattern given a breakout. Turn it around.
byKey.joint: That is breakout and pattern together. Divide by every way the pattern appears.
byKey.base: That is the base rate. The pattern should move it.

explain.text: Breakout and pattern: $0.05 \times 0.6 = 0.03$. Failure and pattern: $0.95 \times 0.1 = 0.095$. So $0.03 / 0.125 = 0.24$.

quiz.prose: A test keeps its hit rate of 90% and false-positive rate of 5%. The condition becomes ten times as common, from 1% to 10%.
quiz.question: What happens to $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$?

options.text: It rises, but by less than ten times

options.why: You kept only the test's rates. The base rate is in the formula too.
The bottom of the fraction grows as well, so the rise is smaller than tenfold.
More people with the condition means more true positives, so it cannot fall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work it out at 1% and at 10%.

explain.text: At 1%: $0.009 / 0.0585 \approx 0.15$. At 10%: $0.09 / 0.135 \approx 0.67$. That is about 4.3 times, not 10.

quiz.prose: Half of the loans in a pool are risky. A credit check flags 80% of risky loans and 20% of safe ones. A loan is flagged.
quiz.question: What is the chance it is risky? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: With an even base rate, it is $0.8 / (0.8 + 0.2)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the two flagged paths.

byKey.base: That is the chance before the check. A flag should move it.
byKey.joint: That is risky and flagged together. Divide by every flag, 0.5.

explain.text: Risky and flagged: $0.5 \times 0.8 = 0.4$. Safe and flagged: $0.5 \times 0.2 = 0.1$. So $0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8$: with a 50% base rate, only the check's two rates matter.

quiz.prose: A test never misses: its hit rate is 100%. It wrongly flags 2% of healthy people. The condition affects 2% of people.
quiz.question: You test positive. What is the chance you have the condition? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of the condition given a positive

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the two positive paths.

byKey.perfect: Never missing a case is not the same as never flagging a healthy person. False positives still come in.
byKey.spec: That is the share of healthy people who test negative. It does not answer the question.
byKey.base: That is the base rate. The positive should raise it.

explain.text: Condition and positive: $0.02 \times 1 = 0.02$. Healthy and positive: $0.98 \times 0.02 = 0.0196$. So a positive is barely better than a coin flip, about 0.505.
